beats.summary: The double has a long literary history (romantic and gothic); literary doubles are imperfect, and the imperfection is the menace.
beats.canonical: The theme of the human double or replica certainly has a long history in film and literature. The double may be artificial, created by a human agent, or the double may be another human, who bears an uncanny and often inexplicable resemblance to the main character. Both kinds of doubles are common in romantic and gothic literature of the nineteenth century. In most of these literary versions, the double is imperfect, less than human or in some disturbing or fantastical way different, and the differences are as much a part of the menace as the resemblance itself.

quotations.text: All such doubles could be understood as literary forerunners of the roboticists' attempts to get to the other side of the uncanny valley.

depth.trigger: Reader asks for examples or knows the literature
depth.material: Poe's William Wilson, Wilde's Dorian Gray, Jekyll and Hyde, Dostoevsky's The Double, Shelley's Frankenstein, and in the German tradition Hoffmann's Der Sandmann. If the reader knows Hoffmann: Olimpia anticipates Ishiguro's android Erica — the automaton tradition continued under laboratory conditions.

deferrals.freud: Freud read Hoffmann too, and the book will come to his essay — but it wants you to see the doubles themselves before the theory that claimed them.
deferrals.ai: Hold that thought. The book will argue that the machine you are now talking to belongs to this lineage, but it has to earn the claim through film first.

beats.exit: Reader has encountered the claim that literary doubles are imperfect and that the imperfection, not just the resemblance, is the menace.

exhibits.cue: Show when examples are requested; period engraving, dark treatment.

beats.summary: Film did not merely inherit the double as a theme; film is itself a technology of doubling, and was received as uncanny from the first.
beats.canonical: The powerful literary tradition is certainly part of the explanation for film's interest in uncanny doubles. But part of the explanation also lies in the nature of film itself as one of Benjamin's technologies of mechanical reproduction. From the first, film was uncanny in that it seemed to reproduce the world even though its audience knew better.

quotations.text: From the first, film was uncanny in that it seemed to reproduce the world even though its audience knew better.

depth.trigger: Reader resists: 'isn't this just a metaphor?'
depth.material: The claim is structural, not figurative: a medium of mechanical reproduction produces a double of the world by its nature. The thematic doubles of the previous beat are film thinking about its own condition. This is the section's pivot, and everything after depends on it.

deferrals.aura: Benjamin is already in the room — the book will take up aura directly once the La Ciotat material is on the table.

beats.exit: Reader can distinguish the double as a theme IN film from film AS a doubling technology.

beats.summary: The story of the audience fleeing the Lumière train is false but functions as a foundation myth; what it remembers is astonishment — knowing-and-not-knowing — not naive fear (Gunning).
beats.canonical: The story was told that at the first showing of The Arrival of a Train in La Ciotat Station in 1896, the audience feared that the train would actually pass through the screen and crush them. But the story should be understood not as an account of what happened, but rather as a kind of foundation myth. Tom Gunning argues that what the myth remembers is not naive fear in the audience, but a more sophisticated reaction, astonishment. The audience knew that they were watching a mediated experience, and yet what they saw on the screen looked more convincingly real than any earlier medium.

quotations.source: Richard Grusin, 'DVDs, Video Games, and the Cinema of Interactions' (2016), quoted in the essay
quotations.text: This aesthetic of astonishment involves a contradictory response to the ontological status of moving photographic images, a response which tries to incorporate two contradictory beliefs or states of mind — the knowledge that one is sitting in a public theater watching an exhibition of a new motion picture technology and the feeling that what one is seeing on screen looks real.

depth.trigger: Reader asks whether audiences were really so naive
depth.material: They were not — that is Gunning's point and the reason the myth matters. The same audiences attended magic theaters; Méliès owned one. They were prepared to receive film as a new kind of magic: astonishment in full knowledge of the trick.

depth.trigger: Reader connects to suspension of disbelief
depth.material: Distinguish the two: suspension of disbelief is a narrative convention the reader agrees to; the aesthetic of astonishment is a perceptual and ontological response to the medium itself. One concerns the story, the other the fact of the moving image.

deferrals.myth-vs-effect: The book is about to give that distinction a name — let it set Gorky beside the myth first.

beats.exit: Reader has encountered the astonishment structure: two contradictory states of mind held at once.

exhibits.cue: Show on first mention of La Ciotat. Same still recurs in the next two beats — repetition with difference.

beats.summary: Gorky felt the gap from the other direction — not almost-too-real but drained of life. The gap must exist for astonishment or unease, but cannot be so large that resemblance is lost.
beats.canonical: The astonishment felt by early film audiences was a positive response to the uncanny resemblance between the filmed world and their experience of the physical world. For some, such as Maxim Gorky, the differences were more disturbing than the resemblance was pleasurable. The gap must exist in order to arouse a reaction of pleasurable astonishment or anxiety, but it cannot be so large that the resemblance is lost.

quotations.source: Maxim Gorky on the Lumière films, quoted via Gunning (2003)
quotations.text: Before you a life is surging, a life deprived of words and shorn of the living spectrum of colors — the gray, soundless, the bleak and dismal life. (…) It is terrifying to see, but it is the movement of shadows, only of shadows.
This asymptotic approach to the reproduction of life produces the effect of the uncanny and phantasmatic.

depth.material: Yes: Gunning is describing film's own uncanny valley, sixty-five years before Mori drew the curve. The word 'asymptotic' is exact — an asymptote approaches but never reaches its target. If the Mori graph exhibit is available, place film on the rising far slope now.

beats.exit: Reader holds both directions of the gap: Lumière astonishment (almost too real) and Gorky unease (conspicuously not real enough).

exhibits.cue: The same still, fully desaturated, contrast lowered. Same frame, different world — the exhibit performs Gorky's reaction rather than illustrating it.
If the persistent Mori curve is implemented, film gets plotted on the far slope at this beat.

beats.summary: The section's central distinction: the La Ciotat MYTH (film could close the gap with the real — never true) versus the La Ciotat EFFECT (the pleasurable or anxious experience of the gap — essential to film). The effect could hardly exist without the myth.
beats.canonical: We can therefore draw a distinction between the La Ciotat myth and the La Ciotat effect. The myth is that film could actually achieve the goal of reproducing the real, and in this sense neither the Lumière brothers nor contemporary film technology could succeed. The La Ciotat effect is the pleasurable or anxious experience of the gap between film and the real. Film never overcame this uncanny valley. In fact, we would argue that the La Ciotat effect is essential to film but that the effect could hardly exist without the myth that lies behind it.

quotations.text: Film never overcame this uncanny valley.

quotations.source: essay, on the persistence of the myth
quotations.text: Even in the twenty-first century, the dominant rhetoric of mainstream or Hollywood film is that it can or might someday be able to close the gap.

depth.trigger: Reader objects: hasn't IMAX / 4K / CGI closed the gap?
depth.material: No audience of an IMAX film is fooled into thinking the action is happening before their eyes. Technical improvement narrows the gap; it cannot abolish it, because the viewer's knowledge that this is a projection is part of the experience. Improvement feeds the myth and sharpens the effect — it does not end either.

depth.trigger: Reader asks why the myth matters if it is false
depth.material: Because the effect depends on it. Astonishment requires the half-belief that the gap might close. A culture that entirely stopped believing the myth would stop feeling the effect — which is why the industry rehearses the myth at every technological generation.

deferrals.ai: Now you have the instrument the book will use everywhere. When it reaches generative AI, the question will be: what is the La Ciotat myth of the machine that converses — and who is telling it? But the book asks for Benjamin first.

beats.exit: Reader can state the distinction in their own words — myth as the impossible promise, effect as the lived experience of the gap — and has seen that the effect needs the myth.

beats.summary: Benjamin's aura, reread: neither aura's presence nor its complete loss is uncanny, but the condition in between — and film (like VR after it) lives permanently in that condition.
beats.canonical: With photography and film, what Benjamin was perhaps describing was not the end of aura, but rather a moment in which the auratic status of art was being challenged. This undermining of aura was a process rather than an accomplished fact. Furthermore, Benjamin did not adequately account for the fact that our media culture seems to want to reinscribe aura rather than banish it entirely. We can still argue that all films exist in a permanent state of losing aura. For it is neither the presence of aura nor its complete disappearance that is uncanny, but the condition in between, which is precisely where film as well as VR applications are located.

quotations.text: aura is, for Benjamin, 'the unique phenomenon of a distance, however close it may be'

depth.trigger: Reader knows the Artwork essay well
depth.material: Acknowledge the ambiguity in Benjamin: at times the essay says reproduction destroys aura by nature; elsewhere (and in the Short History of Photography) technique can fashion or drain aura — Atget draining the streets of Paris. The essay's move: Benjamin could name aura precisely because it was newly threatened. And the culture re-auratizes: film stars became auratic objects in the 1930s.

beats.exit: Reader has the in-between formulation: permanent crisis of aura as the home of the uncanny.

exhibits.cue: Optional, on the Atget point only.

beats.summary: Freud's uncanny and the fetish as substitute: filmic doubling substitutes the viewing of film for the world; mainstream film remains uncanny because it purports to be what we know it is not.
beats.canonical: Freud begins his analysis by noting that the word uncanny, in German unheimlich, has itself a rather uncanny semantic field. The uncanny, Freud argues, has a double quality: it is the feeling that something is hiding beneath the surface, something both familiar and strange. We need not accept his reductionist explanation to appreciate his observations about the double character of the uncanny or the fetish as substitutes. Filmic doubling substitutes our experience of viewing film for our experience of the real world.

quotations.text: Mainstream film remains uncanny because it purports to be what we know it is not.

depth.material: The essay keeps Freud's observation and drops his mechanism: the double character of the uncanny and the substitute-structure of the fetish survive; the castration explanation does not — the essay calls it reductionist and sexist directly. (In the book's larger argument, Jentsch's uncertainty-about-animacy will do the work Freud claimed; this section uses only what Freud earns here.)

deferrals.deepfakes: The fetish-substitute structure returns when the book reaches deepfakes — it is doing local work here.

beats.exit: Reader has the substitution structure: the double stands in for the real, and the standing-in is what we both know and forget.
